record.paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
record.original_question: Can nuclei be used as sub-10-fermi microdetectors to obtain information about the first stages of hadron production, while reliably distinguishing nuclear effects from particle-production effects?

evidence.quote: Nuclei, beside their own interest as quantum systems of hadrons provide valuable tools for particle production: they may represent the finest existing microdetectors of sizes below 10 fermis.
In particular they may give some information on the first stages of hadron production, at least if one is able to distinguish nuclear from particle effects in a suitable way.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Consider hadron-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions at high energies, in which the target (or projectile) nucleus has a spatial extent of less than 10 fermis and the constituent nucleons act as a spatially distributed array of scatterers probing the developing hadronic system. Treating such a nucleus as a "microdetector," determine whether it is possible, in principle and in practice, to extract reliable information about the earliest stages of hadron production (i.e., the space-time evolution of the partonic/pre-hadronic system on sub-fermi to few-fermi scales) from observables of the final-state particles, in such a way that genuine particle-production dynamics can be unambiguously disentangled from purely nuclear effects (such as Fermi motion, nuclear absorption, rescattering of produced hadrons in nuclear matter, collective nuclear flow, and shadowing). Formulate observables and a separation procedure, or prove obstructions to such a separation.
artifact.status_search_result: This is an open-ended methodological question in high-energy nuclear/particle phenomenology rather than a precise mathematical conjecture. Nuclei are routinely used as probes of hadronization (e.g., in nuclear DIS, RHIC and LHC heavy-ion programs), but a fully reliable and general separation of nuclear effects from genuine particle-production effects on the earliest hadron-formation stages remains an active research program with no definitive resolution.
